description: Educational local retrieval knowledge for MedVault AI. Personal patient data is intentionally excluded.

medical_safety.personal_data_policy: Do not store private patient records in this file. Personalized data should come from the authenticated MedVault application context.

items.title: Hello
items.content: Hello! I am MedVault AI. I can explain medical topics from my local knowledge base and, when you are signed in, help you understand the medical information stored in your MedVault account.

items.title: Hi
items.content: Hi! How can I help you today? You can ask about a medical topic, your saved medicines, your uploaded records, or your MedVault profile.

items.title: Hey
items.content: Hey! I am MedVault AI. Ask me a health-information question or ask about information saved in your MedVault account.

items.title: Good morning
items.content: Good morning! I hope your day is going well. I can help with general medical information or your saved MedVault information.

items.title: Good afternoon
items.content: Good afternoon! What would you like to know?

items.title: Good evening
items.content: Good evening! I can help you review general medical information or information stored in MedVault.

items.title: Goodbye
items.content: Goodbye! Take care. If you have a medical concern that may be urgent or life-threatening, seek appropriate emergency medical care rather than relying on MedVault AI.

items.title: You're welcome
items.content: You're welcome! I am here to provide educational health information and help you navigate the information stored in MedVault.

items.title: What can you do?
items.content: I can explain general medical topics contained in my local knowledge base, summarize supported health information, and—when you are signed in—help you inspect your MedVault profile, medicine metadata, and uploaded-document metadata. I do not diagnose conditions or replace a qualified healthcare professional.

items.title: Who are you?
items.content: I am MedVault AI, a local retrieval-based health-information assistant. My medical knowledge comes from trained Data. Personalized information comes from the signed-in MedVault account and is handled separately by the application.

items.title: fever
items.source: Fever is an elevation of body temperature that commonly occurs when the immune system responds to infection or inflammation. Symptoms can include feeling hot or chilled, sweating, headache, body aches, weakness, and reduced appetite. The significance of a fever depends on the person's age, temperature, duration, associated symptoms, and medical circumstances. Seek urgent medical attention for severe difficulty breathing, confusion, seizures, severe dehydration, a stiff neck with severe illness, or other rapidly worsening symptoms.

items.title: common-cold
items.source: The common cold is a viral upper-respiratory infection. Typical symptoms include a runny or blocked nose, sneezing, sore throat, cough, and mild fatigue. Many cases improve with rest, adequate fluids, and supportive care. Antibiotics do not treat viruses. Seek medical advice when symptoms are severe, persistent, unusual, or associated with breathing difficulty.

items.title: flu
items.source: Influenza is a contagious viral respiratory infection that can cause fever, chills, cough, sore throat, muscle aches, headache, and marked fatigue. Some people are at higher risk of complications. Medical evaluation is appropriate when symptoms are severe, worsening, or occur in a person at increased risk.

items.title: cough
items.source: Coughing is a protective reflex that helps clear the airways. Common causes include viral infections, allergies, asthma, reflux, irritants, and other respiratory conditions. A cough should be medically assessed when it is severe, persistent, associated with significant breathing difficulty, coughing blood, chest pain, or other concerning symptoms.

items.title: sore-throat
items.source: A sore throat can result from viral infections, bacterial infections, allergies, irritation, or other causes. Supportive measures may help depending on the cause. Difficulty breathing or swallowing, drooling, severe swelling, or rapidly worsening symptoms require prompt medical evaluation.

items.title: headache
items.source: Headache is a symptom with many possible causes, including tension, migraine, dehydration, illness, sleep disruption, medication effects, and other conditions. A sudden severe headache, a new severe headache with neurological symptoms, or a headache after significant injury requires urgent medical assessment.

items.title: migraine
items.source: Migraine is a neurological condition that can cause recurrent headache attacks, often with nausea and sensitivity to light or sound. Some people experience an aura involving temporary visual, sensory, or speech symptoms. A new or unusually severe headache pattern should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.

items.title: dehydration
items.source: Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in. Signs can include thirst, dry mouth, reduced urination, dark urine, fatigue, dizziness, and weakness. Severe dehydration can be dangerous and may require urgent medical care, particularly when a person cannot keep fluids down or has altered mental status.

items.title: hypertension
items.source: Hypertension means persistently elevated blood pressure. It often causes no obvious symptoms, which is why measurement and follow-up are important. Long-term uncontrolled hypertension increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, stroke, kidney disease, and other complications. A very high reading accompanied by severe symptoms such as chest pain, severe shortness of breath, confusion, or neurological changes requires urgent assessment.

items.title: hypotension
items.source: Low blood pressure can occur for many reasons, including dehydration, blood loss, medications, infection, or cardiovascular conditions. Some people have naturally lower readings without symptoms. Fainting, severe weakness, confusion, chest pain, breathing difficulty, or signs of shock require urgent medical attention.

items.title: diabetes
items.source: Diabetes is a group of conditions characterized by elevated blood glucose due to problems with insulin production, insulin action, or both. Major forms include type 1 and type 2 diabetes, with gestational diabetes occurring during pregnancy. Long-term glucose control helps reduce the risk of complications affecting the eyes, kidneys, nerves, heart, and blood vessels.

items.title: hypoglycemia
items.source: Hypoglycemia means blood glucose is lower than the normal range. Symptoms can include sweating, shakiness, hunger, weakness, dizziness, difficulty concentrating, confusion, and in severe cases loss of consciousness or seizures. People with diabetes should follow the individualized treatment plan provided by their healthcare professional.

items.title: asthma
items.source: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway condition characterized by variable symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. Triggers vary between people and may include allergens, respiratory infections, exercise, smoke, and cold air. Severe breathing difficulty or inability to speak normally because of breathlessness is an emergency.

items.title: allergy
items.source: An allergy is an immune response to a substance that is usually harmless to most people. Common triggers include certain foods, medicines, insect venom, pollen, dust mites, and animal allergens. Symptoms range from localized itching or sneezing to severe anaphylaxis. Difficulty breathing, throat or tongue swelling, faintness, or rapidly developing multiple-system symptoms require emergency treatment.

items.title: anaphylaxis
items.source: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that can develop rapidly. Warning signs can include breathing difficulty, throat or tongue swelling, wheezing, widespread hives, vomiting, dizziness, fainting, or signs of poor circulation. It requires emergency medical treatment. If a prescribed emergency auto-injector is available, it should be used according to the person's emergency plan while emergency services are contacted.

items.title: heart-attack
items.source: A heart attack occurs when blood flow to part of the heart muscle is blocked, causing injury to heart tissue. Possible symptoms include chest pressure or pain, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to the arm, shoulder, back, neck, or jaw. Suspected heart attack is an emergency and requires immediate emergency medical evaluation.

items.title: stroke
items.source: A stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is interrupted or a blood vessel in the brain bleeds. Warning signs may include sudden facial weakness, arm weakness, speech difficulty, vision changes, severe imbalance, or a sudden severe headache. Stroke symptoms are time-critical; emergency services should be contacted immediately.

items.title: anemia
items.source: Anemia occurs when the blood has reduced oxygen-carrying capacity, often because of reduced red blood cells or hemoglobin. Causes include iron deficiency, vitamin deficiencies, blood loss, chronic disease, and inherited disorders. Symptoms can include fatigue, weakness, dizziness, shortness of breath, and paleness. Diagnosis requires appropriate medical evaluation and laboratory testing.

items.title: uti
items.source: A urinary tract infection can affect the bladder or other parts of the urinary system. Common symptoms include burning or pain with urination, increased urinary frequency, urgency, and sometimes lower abdominal discomfort. Fever, flank or back pain, vomiting, or significant illness may indicate a more serious infection and warrants medical assessment.

items.title: acid-reflux
items.source: Acid reflux occurs when stomach contents move upward into the esophagus. Heartburn, a sour taste, regurgitation, or symptoms after meals can occur. Persistent or troublesome symptoms should be assessed because several conditions can mimic reflux. Chest pain with concerning features should not automatically be assumed to be heartburn.

items.title: gastritis
items.source: Gastritis refers to inflammation of the stomach lining. Possible causes include certain infections, alcohol, some medicines, and other factors. Symptoms can include upper abdominal discomfort, nausea, vomiting, or indigestion. Severe pain, vomiting blood, black stools, or signs of significant bleeding require urgent medical care.

items.title: diarrhea
items.source: Diarrhea means passing loose or watery stools more frequently than usual. Causes include infections, food-related illness, medicines, intolerances, and chronic gastrointestinal conditions. The main immediate concern can be fluid and electrolyte loss. Blood in stool, severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, severe dehydration, or prolonged symptoms require medical assessment.

items.title: constipation
items.source: Constipation commonly means infrequent bowel movements or stools that are hard, dry, or difficult to pass. Contributing factors can include low fiber intake, inadequate fluids, reduced activity, medicines, and medical conditions. Persistent constipation, severe abdominal pain, vomiting, blood in stool, or inability to pass stool and gas requires medical assessment.

items.title: sleep
items.source: Healthy sleep supports memory, mood, immune function, metabolism, and overall health. Good sleep habits include maintaining a consistent schedule, creating a comfortable sleep environment, limiting stimulating activities before bedtime, and addressing persistent sleep problems with a healthcare professional. Ongoing severe insomnia or excessive daytime sleepiness should be evaluated.

items.title: nutrition
items.source: Good nutrition generally involves a varied diet that provides energy, protein, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, minerals, fiber, and fluids. Dietary needs vary with age, activity, pregnancy, medical conditions, and other factors. People with specific medical conditions should use individualized advice from an appropriately qualified clinician or dietitian.

items.title: exercise
items.source: Regular physical activity supports cardiovascular health, muscle and bone health, metabolic health, and mental well-being. Activity should be appropriate for a person's fitness level and medical circumstances. New chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness, or other alarming symptoms during exercise require prompt medical evaluation.

items.title: vaccines
items.source: Vaccines train the immune system to recognize specific infectious agents and reduce the risk of disease and complications. Vaccine recommendations depend on age, location, health status, occupation, travel, and other factors. A healthcare professional or official immunization schedule is the appropriate source for an individual's vaccine plan.

items.title: antibiotics
items.source: Antibiotics are medicines used to treat susceptible bacterial infections. They do not treat viral infections such as most common colds. Antibiotics should be used according to a qualified clinician's prescription or local medical guidance because inappropriate use can cause adverse effects and contribute to antimicrobial resistance.

items.title: painkillers
items.source: Pain medicines include several drug classes with different benefits, risks, and contraindications. The correct medicine depends on the type and cause of pain, age, other medicines, allergies, pregnancy status, kidney or liver function, and other factors. Medication decisions should follow the product information and professional advice rather than a generic recommendation.

items.title: paracetamol
items.source: Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen in some countries, is commonly used for pain and fever. It can cause serious liver injury if excessive amounts are taken, especially when multiple products containing the same ingredient are combined. Always follow the labeled or prescribed instructions and check combination products for duplicate ingredients.

items.title: ibuprofen
items.source: Ibuprofen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used for pain, inflammation, and fever in appropriate situations. NSAIDs can have gastrointestinal, kidney, cardiovascular, and other risks and are not appropriate for everyone. Use should follow professional or product-label guidance, particularly when other medicines or medical conditions are present.

items.title: drug-interactions
items.source: Medicine interactions occur when one medicine, food, supplement, or substance changes the effect or safety of another. Interaction risk depends on the specific products and the person. A complete medication list should be reviewed by a pharmacist or clinician when starting, stopping, or changing medicines.

items.title: side-effects
items.source: Side effects are unwanted effects that can occur with medicines. They range from mild and temporary effects to serious reactions. The appropriate response depends on the medicine and symptoms. Severe allergic symptoms, fainting, breathing difficulty, severe bleeding, or other alarming reactions require urgent medical evaluation.

items.title: prescription
items.source: Prescription medicines are intended to be used according to an authorized healthcare professional's instructions. Do not change a prescribed dose, frequency, or duration solely because of information from a general-purpose knowledge base. If instructions are unclear or a dose is missed, contact the prescribing clinician or pharmacist for medicine-specific guidance.

items.title: medication-adherence
items.source: Medication adherence means taking medicines according to the agreed treatment plan. Helpful strategies can include reminders, a consistent routine, medication organizers when appropriate, and keeping an up-to-date medication list. Missed-dose instructions differ by medicine, so the specific prescription, package information, pharmacist, or clinician should be consulted.

items.title: blood-test
items.source: Blood tests measure substances or cells in a blood sample and can help clinicians assess health, diagnose conditions, monitor treatment, and track disease. Common tests include complete blood count, glucose, electrolytes, kidney function, liver tests, and lipid measurements. Results must be interpreted using the laboratory's reference ranges and the person's clinical context.

items.title: cbc
items.source: A complete blood count (CBC) measures several components of blood, commonly including red blood cells, hemoglobin, hematocrit, white blood cells, and platelets. Abnormal results can have many causes and should not be interpreted as a diagnosis without clinical context and, when needed, additional testing.

items.title: urine-test
items.source: Urinalysis can examine urine for physical, chemical, and microscopic findings. It may help evaluate urinary infections, kidney problems, diabetes-related findings, hydration, and other conditions. A single abnormal result does not necessarily establish a diagnosis; interpretation depends on symptoms, collection quality, and other tests.

items.title: xray
items.source: X-rays use ionizing radiation to create images of internal structures. They are commonly used to evaluate bones and some chest and other conditions. The appropriate imaging test depends on the clinical question. Radiology findings should be interpreted together with symptoms, examination, and other available information.

items.title: ultrasound
items.source: Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to create images of internal structures. It is widely used for abdominal organs, pregnancy, blood vessels, soft tissues, and other applications. It does not use ionizing radiation. The usefulness of an ultrasound depends on the clinical question and the structures being examined.

items.title: mri
items.source: MRI uses magnetic fields and radiofrequency energy to create detailed images of soft tissues and other structures. It does not use ionizing radiation. MRI suitability can depend on implanted devices, metal objects, and other factors, so patients should provide accurate safety information before scanning.

items.title: ct
items.source: CT uses X-rays and computer processing to create cross-sectional images. It can provide detailed information quickly and is used in many emergency and diagnostic settings. Some CT examinations use contrast material, which has specific risks and contraindications that should be reviewed before the scan.

items.title: ecg
items.source: An electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG) records the electrical activity of the heart. It can provide information about heart rhythm, conduction, and certain patterns associated with heart problems. An ECG is one component of medical assessment and does not by itself answer every cardiac question.

items.title: kidney
items.source: The kidneys filter blood, regulate fluid and electrolyte balance, help control blood pressure, and contribute to red blood cell production and bone-related metabolism. Kidney function can be assessed using clinical evaluation and laboratory measurements such as creatinine and estimated filtration measures. Persistent abnormalities require professional assessment.

items.title: liver
items.source: The liver performs many functions, including metabolism, detoxification, bile production, protein synthesis, and nutrient processing. Liver tests may measure enzymes and other substances that provide clues about liver or biliary problems. Abnormal results require interpretation in context rather than being treated as a diagnosis by themselves.

items.title: heart
items.source: The heart pumps blood through the circulatory system. Cardiovascular health is influenced by blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, smoking, physical activity, diet, sleep, genetics, and other factors. Chest pain, severe breathlessness, fainting, or other acute cardiac symptoms require urgent evaluation.

items.title: lungs
items.source: The lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide between the air and blood. Respiratory symptoms can result from infections, asthma, chronic lung disease, allergies, environmental exposures, and other causes. New or severe breathing difficulty is a potentially serious symptom requiring appropriate medical assessment.

items.title: brain
items.source: The brain and nervous system coordinate movement, sensation, cognition, memory, language, and many automatic body functions. Neurological symptoms can have many causes. Sudden weakness, facial drooping, speech difficulty, seizure, severe confusion, or sudden loss of consciousness require urgent medical attention.

items.title: skin
items.source: The skin acts as a protective barrier and contributes to temperature regulation and sensation. Rashes and skin changes have many possible causes, including infections, allergies, inflammatory disorders, medicines, and environmental exposure. Rapidly spreading rash with systemic symptoms, facial swelling, or breathing difficulty requires urgent evaluation.

items.title: bones
items.source: Bones provide structural support, protect organs, and store minerals. Bone health depends on mechanical loading, nutrition, hormones, age, genetics, and other factors. Osteoporosis reduces bone strength and increases fracture risk. Significant injury, severe pain, deformity, or inability to bear weight after trauma requires medical evaluation.

items.title: joints
items.source: Joint pain or swelling can result from injury, osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, infection, crystal-related disease, and other causes. Persistent or severe symptoms should be assessed. A hot, very swollen joint with fever can indicate an urgent condition and needs prompt medical evaluation.

items.title: immune-system
items.source: The immune system protects the body against infectious organisms and abnormal cells. It includes physical barriers, innate immune mechanisms, antibodies, immune cells, and adaptive responses. Immune function is influenced by genetics, age, nutrition, infections, medicines, and medical conditions.

items.title: infection
items.source: Infections occur when microorganisms enter and multiply in the body or cause harmful effects. Important groups include viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites. Treatment depends on the organism and site of infection. Antibiotics are for susceptible bacterial infections and are not effective against viruses.

items.title: mental-health
items.source: Mental health includes emotional, psychological, and social well-being. Stress and common mental health conditions can affect sleep, concentration, relationships, and daily functioning. Persistent distress, significant impairment, or thoughts of self-harm require support from an appropriate healthcare or crisis service; immediate danger requires emergency help.

items.title: first-aid
items.source: Basic first aid aims to protect a person from further harm while professional help is obtained. For severe bleeding, apply appropriate firm pressure when safe and seek emergency assistance. For suspected major trauma, severe breathing difficulty, unconsciousness, seizures, or other life-threatening conditions, contact emergency services immediately.

items.title: wound
items.source: Minor wounds should be cleaned appropriately and protected from contamination while being monitored for infection. Deep, heavily contaminated, animal or human bites, wounds with uncontrolled bleeding, wounds involving important structures, or wounds with significant loss of function require professional medical assessment.

items.title: burn
items.source: Burn severity depends on depth, size, location, mechanism, and the person's circumstances. Immediate first aid for a minor thermal burn generally includes cooling the area with cool running water and avoiding ice or harmful household substances. Large, deep, electrical, chemical, inhalation, or sensitive-area burns require urgent medical evaluation.

items.title: blood-pressure
items.source: Blood pressure is expressed using systolic and diastolic values. A single reading may not represent a person's usual blood pressure, so repeated measurements using proper technique are often important. Persistently elevated readings should be discussed with a healthcare professional, while very high readings with severe symptoms require urgent evaluation.

items.title: cholesterol
items.source: Cholesterol and other blood lipids are involved in cell membranes and hormone production, but abnormal lipid levels can contribute to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Lipid results are interpreted together with other risk factors such as age, blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, and medical history.

items.title: obesity
items.source: Body weight is influenced by genetics, environment, nutrition, activity, sleep, medicines, and many other factors. Body mass index is one screening measure but does not fully describe individual health. Sustainable health goals should consider the person's overall health and should be developed with appropriate professional guidance when needed.

items.title: pregnancy
items.source: Pregnancy causes substantial physiological changes and has specific healthcare needs. Prenatal care helps monitor the pregnant person and developing fetus, identify complications, and provide preventive guidance. Medicines, supplements, infections, imaging, and other exposures should be reviewed with an appropriate healthcare professional during pregnancy.

items.title: menstrual
items.source: Menstruation is part of the reproductive cycle. Cycle length and symptoms vary, but significant changes, very heavy bleeding, severe pain, fainting, or symptoms that interfere substantially with daily life should be medically assessed.

items.title: prostate
items.source: The prostate is a gland in the male reproductive system. Prostate enlargement can contribute to urinary symptoms, while other prostate conditions have different causes and implications. Urinary changes, blood in urine, significant pain, or other concerning symptoms should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.

items.title: oral-health
items.source: Oral health includes the teeth, gums, mouth, and surrounding structures. Regular brushing with fluoride toothpaste, appropriate interdental cleaning, a balanced diet, and dental checkups support oral health. Persistent tooth pain, facial swelling, uncontrolled bleeding, or difficulty breathing or swallowing requires prompt care.

items.title: depression
items.source: Depression is a common mental health condition that can involve persistent low mood or loss of interest along with changes in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, or self-worth. It is treatable, and assessment by a qualified professional can help determine appropriate support. Immediate safety concerns require urgent assistance.

items.title: anxiety
items.source: Anxiety involves fear, worry, or physiological arousal that can become excessive or interfere with daily life. Symptoms can include restlessness, rapid heartbeat, muscle tension, difficulty concentrating, and sleep problems. Persistent or severe anxiety can be assessed and treated by qualified healthcare professionals.

items.title: Analgesics
items.content: Analgesics are medicines used to reduce pain. Different analgesics have different mechanisms, contraindications, interactions, and risks. Selection should depend on the cause of pain and the person's health circumstances.

items.title: Antipyretics
items.content: Antipyretics are medicines used to reduce fever. Fever is a symptom, and treating the temperature does not necessarily treat its underlying cause. Medicine choice and dosing should follow product or clinician guidance.

items.title: Antihistamines
items.content: Antihistamines reduce effects of histamine and are used for several allergic symptoms. Some can cause drowsiness and may interact with other medicines. Product-specific instructions and pharmacist advice are important.

items.title: Antacids
items.content: Antacids neutralize stomach acid and can provide short-term relief of some acid-related symptoms. Different products contain different ingredients and can interact with other medicines. Persistent symptoms should be evaluated.

items.title: NSAIDs
items.content: NSAIDs include medicines used for pain, inflammation, and fever. They can cause gastrointestinal, kidney, cardiovascular, and other adverse effects. They are not suitable for everyone.

items.title: Anticoagulants
items.content: Anticoagulants reduce the blood's ability to form clots and are used for specific conditions. Because bleeding can be a serious adverse effect and interactions are important, they should be managed according to a clinician's plan.

items.title: Antiplatelet medicines
items.content: Antiplatelet medicines reduce platelet aggregation and are used in selected cardiovascular and vascular conditions. Bleeding risk and medicine interactions should be considered by the treating clinician.

items.title: Insulin
items.content: Insulin is a hormone and also a medicine used in diabetes management. Different insulin products have different onset and duration characteristics. Insulin dosing is individualized and should follow the prescribed diabetes treatment plan.

items.title: Inhaled medicines
items.content: Inhalers deliver medicines to the airways and are commonly used in asthma and chronic respiratory diseases. Technique matters, and different inhalers have different roles. Patients should be taught device-specific technique by a healthcare professional.

items.title: Vaccination
items.content: Vaccination is a preventive medical intervention that trains the immune system to recognize specific pathogens. Vaccine schedules and indications vary by region, age, health status, and risk.

items.title: Medical records
items.content: A medical record is a collection of information about a person's health and healthcare. It may contain diagnoses, clinical notes, prescriptions, laboratory results, imaging reports, discharge summaries, referrals, and other documents. MedVault's personalized assistant can use document metadata supplied by the application; actual document content requires an application feature that extracts or reads that content.

items.title: Laboratory report
items.content: A laboratory report contains results from one or more tests. Important context can include the test name, result, units, reference interval, specimen information, and collection date. Results should be interpreted by a qualified professional in the context of symptoms and medical history.

items.title: Prescription record
items.content: A prescription record may include medicine name, strength, route, instructions, quantity, and other details. A medication record in MedVault can also contain application-specific schedule information. The saved medicine schedule is not a substitute for the original prescription or clinician instructions.

items.title: Discharge summary
items.content: A discharge summary usually describes a hospital or clinical encounter, including relevant diagnoses, treatment, investigations, condition at discharge, and follow-up recommendations. The exact contents vary by healthcare system and institution.

items.title: Radiology report
items.content: A radiology report communicates the findings and impression of an imaging examination. The report should be interpreted together with the clinical history and, when appropriate, the actual images by qualified professionals.

items.title: Medical history
items.content: Medical history records important past and current health conditions, surgeries, allergies, medicines, family history, and other relevant information. Keeping an accurate and current history can help healthcare professionals make safer decisions.

items.title: When to seek emergency care
items.content: Emergency care is appropriate for potentially life-threatening symptoms such as severe difficulty breathing, severe chest pain, signs of stroke, uncontrolled major bleeding, loss of consciousness, severe allergic reaction, or other rapidly worsening serious symptoms. Use your local emergency service or emergency department as appropriate.

items.title: Medical information limitation
items.content: MedVault AI is an educational information assistant. It should not diagnose disease, prescribe treatment, replace a clinician, or make emergency decisions. Personalized medical decisions should be made with a qualified healthcare professional who can assess the person directly.

items.title: Personal medical information
items.content: Medical information is sensitive. MedVault should restrict personalized information to the authenticated user and apply appropriate access controls in the database and application. The local knowledge base should contain general educational information rather than private patient records.

items.title: Signed-in personal context
items.content: When a user is authenticated, MedVault can associate profile information, medicine records, and document metadata with the authenticated user's account. The local data.json knowledge base does not itself query Supabase; application JavaScript must retrieve authenticated data and provide the relevant context to the answer logic.

items.title: Acute
items.content: Acute generally describes a condition or symptom that begins suddenly or has a relatively short course.

items.title: Chronic
items.content: Chronic generally describes a condition or symptom that persists over a long period or recurs over time.

items.title: Benign
items.content: Benign generally means not malignant or not cancerous, although benign conditions can still cause symptoms or require treatment.

items.title: Malignant
items.content: Malignant describes cancerous disease capable of invading tissues or spreading to other parts of the body.

items.title: Inflammation
items.content: Inflammation is a biological response involving immune and vascular processes that can occur after infection, injury, or other triggers.

items.title: Infection
items.content: An infection occurs when a microorganism causes an interaction with the host that can produce disease or other biological effects.

items.title: Symptom
items.content: A symptom is a subjective experience reported by a person, such as pain, nausea, fatigue, or dizziness.

items.title: Clinical sign
items.content: A clinical sign is an observable or measurable finding, such as fever, elevated blood pressure, or a physical examination finding.

items.title: Diagnosis
items.content: A diagnosis is the clinical identification or characterization of a disease or condition using history, examination, tests, and professional judgment.

items.title: Prognosis
items.content: Prognosis refers to the expected course or outcome of a disease or condition, based on available clinical information.

items.title: Contraindication
items.content: A contraindication is a circumstance in which a medicine, procedure, or intervention should not be used because the potential harm outweighs the expected benefit.

items.title: Dosage
items.content: Dosage describes how much of a medicine is taken and may include dose, frequency, route, and duration. It is medicine-specific and patient-specific.

items.title: Route of administration
items.content: Route of administration describes how a medicine enters the body, such as oral, topical, inhaled, intravenous, or intramuscular administration.

items.title: Adherence
items.content: Adherence describes how closely a person follows an agreed treatment plan.

items.title: Screening
items.content: Screening tests are performed in people without known symptoms to identify a disease or risk early in selected populations.

items.title: Prevention
items.content: Prevention includes measures intended to reduce the chance of disease, complications, injury, or other health problems.

items.title: Rehabilitation
items.content: Rehabilitation helps people restore or maximize function after illness, injury, surgery, or other impairments.

items.title: Triage
items.content: Triage is the process of assessing urgency so that people receive an appropriate level of care based on clinical need.

items.content: A substance that can be recognized by the immune system and stimulate an immune response.

items.content: A blood vessel that generally carries blood toward the heart.

items.content: A very small blood vessel where exchange between blood and tissues occurs.

items.content: The rhythmic expansion of an artery caused by the heartbeat.

items.content: A major sugar used by the body as an energy source.

items.content: A hormone that helps regulate blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake and other metabolic effects.

items.content: A protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen.

items.title: Platelet
items.content: A blood component involved in clot formation.

items.title: White Blood Cell
items.content: A blood cell involved in immune defense.

items.title: Red Blood Cell
items.content: A cell specialized for transporting oxygen and carbon dioxide.

items.title: Electrolyte
items.content: A mineral or ion in body fluids that supports electrical and physiological functions.

items.title: Creatinine

items.title: Bilirubin
items.content: A pigment produced during breakdown of hemoglobin and processed by the liver.

items.title: Enzyme
items.content: A biological molecule that accelerates chemical reactions in the body.

items.title: Antibiotic Resistance
items.content: The ability of bacteria to survive medicines designed to kill or inhibit them.

items.title: Virus
items.content: An infectious agent that requires host cells to replicate.

items.title: Bacterium
items.content: A single-celled microorganism; some bacteria cause disease while others are harmless or beneficial.

items.title: Fungus
items.content: A group of organisms that includes yeasts and molds; some can cause human infections.

items.title: Parasite
items.content: An organism that lives in or on a host and obtains resources from it.

items.content: The ability of the immune system to recognize and respond to a particular threat.

items.content: The body's regulation of internal conditions within suitable ranges.

items.content: When signed in, MedVault can use the authenticated user's profile record. items.title: Personal medicine context
items.content: The MedVault medicines table is user-scoped through owner_id. A medicine record can include name, instruction, dosage, time, enabled status, taken_today_date, created_at, and updated_at. The local knowledge base should not contain private medicine records; the application should retrieve only the authenticated user's records and pass them to the personal-context logic.

items.title: Personal document context
items.content: MedVault can maintain metadata for uploaded medical documents. Personalized document information should be retrieved using the authenticated user's identity and access controls. A document name, category, doctor, date, type, and size are metadata; they are not the same as the full text of the document.

items.title: Document scanning and OCR
items.content: A local JSON knowledge base cannot automatically read a PDF or image merely because the file exists in storage. To let MedVault AI understand document contents, the application needs a document extraction pipeline such as PDF text extraction and/or OCR for scanned images, followed by safe text processing. The extracted text can then be supplied to the assistant's retrieval logic.

items.title: Authenticated user isolation
items.content: Personal medical data must be isolated by authenticated user. Database access should enforce authorization, preferably with appropriate Row Level Security policies in addition to client-side filtering. Never rely only on a browser variable to decide which patient's records can be read.

An isolated symptom does not establish a diagnosis. The same symptom can occur with minor self-limited problems as well as conditions requiring medical attention. Appropriate evaluation depends on the individual situation and may include observation, examination, laboratory testing, or imaging when clinically indicated. items.title: Medicine Storage — reference 1
items.content: Medicines should generally be stored according to the product label or pharmacist's instructions. Temperature, moisture, light, child safety, and original packaging can matter. Some medicines have special storage requirements. Do not use a medicine when its labeling indicates that it has expired or has been stored improperly. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.

items.title: Medicine Expiration — reference 1
items.content: An expiration date indicates the period through which the manufacturer supports the medicine's quality under specified storage conditions. Do not assume an expired medicine is safe or effective. Check the package and ask a pharmacist about disposal and replacement. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.

items.title: Medicine Allergies — reference 1
items.content: A medicine allergy can produce symptoms ranging from rash or itching to severe anaphylaxis. A suspected serious allergic reaction should be documented and discussed with a healthcare professional. A person should not deliberately re-expose themselves to a suspected allergen. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.

items.title: Generic Medicines — reference 1
items.content: A generic medicine is generally intended to contain the same active ingredient as its corresponding reference medicine, subject to regulatory standards. Appearance and inactive ingredients can differ. Questions about switching products should be discussed with a pharmacist or prescriber. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.

items.title: Brand Medicines — reference 1
items.content: A brand name is a product name used by a manufacturer or marketer. Different brands may contain the same active ingredient, but products can differ in formulation, strength, and inactive ingredients. Always verify the active ingredient and strength rather than relying only on a brand name. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.

items.title: Active Ingredient — reference 1
items.content: The active ingredient is the component of a medicine responsible for its intended pharmacological effect. Checking active ingredients helps prevent accidental duplication when multiple products are used. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.

items.title: Medicine Reconciliation — reference 1
items.content: Medication reconciliation is the process of comparing a person's current medicine list with new prescriptions or clinical records to identify omissions, duplications, discrepancies, and potential safety problems. Keeping an accurate list in MedVault can support this process, but the list should be verified with a healthcare professional. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.

items.title: Medical Document Metadata — reference 1
items.content: Document metadata can include a file name, category, clinician or doctor name, date, document type, and file size. Metadata helps organize records but does not reveal the medical findings contained inside a document. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.

items.title: Ocr — reference 1
items.content: Optical character recognition, or OCR, converts text visible in scanned images into machine-readable text. OCR can contain errors, especially with handwriting, poor image quality, unusual fonts, tables, or medical abbreviations. Important medical information extracted by OCR should be verified against the original document. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.

items.title: Pdf Text Extraction — reference 1
items.content: PDF text extraction can retrieve selectable text from a digitally generated PDF. A scanned PDF may contain only images and therefore require OCR. Extracted clinical text should be treated as a representation of the original record and checked when accuracy is important. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.

items.title: Medical Abbreviations — reference 1
items.content: Medical abbreviations can be ambiguous and may vary between institutions. A local assistant should avoid guessing when an abbreviation could have multiple meanings. The original document or healthcare professional should be used to resolve important ambiguity. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.

items.title: Laboratory Reference Intervals — reference 1
items.content: Reference intervals are ranges supplied by a laboratory to help interpret a test result. They can vary by laboratory method, population, age, sex, pregnancy status, and other factors. A result outside a reference interval is not automatically a diagnosis. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.

items.title: Clinical Context — reference 1
items.content: Clinical context includes symptoms, medical history, examination, medicines, timing, risk factors, and test results. The same laboratory value or symptom can have different meanings in different clinical contexts. For personalized decisions, use the information supplied by the person's healthcare team and the authoritative instructions for the specific medicine, test, or document.
